title: Hypoplastic Left Heart Syndrome: Anatomy and Norwood Staging
subject: ss-paediatric-cardiology

steps.say: In the most severe single ventricle lesion the entire left side of the heart is a miniature that can neither receive nor eject blood.
steps.tx: Anatomy defines **hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS core defects)**. Hypoplastic left heart syndrome encompasses aortic atresia or stenosis, mitral atresia or stenosis, a hypoplastic diminutive left ventricle, and severe hypoplasia of the ascending aorta, leaving the right ventricle as the sole functional pumping chamber.

vis.caption: Congenital septal defects including membranous ventricular septal defect with left-to-right shunting. Illustration: StewardMD original.
vis.alt: Diagram of ventricular septal defect showing left-to-right shunt and ventricular anatomy.

steps.say: With no forward flow through the aorta, the brain and coronaries drink backwards through the ductus, which is why closure is instantly fatal.
steps.tx: Perfusion is **duct-dependent systemic flow (retrograde)**. Systemic circulation is entirely ductus dependent, with right ventricular blood traversing the patent ductus retrograde into the aortic arch to perfuse the coronaries and cerebral vessels, so prostaglandin infusion is life support until stage one surgery.

nodes.label: Right ventricle ejects combined output into the pulmonary trunk
Ductus arteriosus carries flow retrograde up the tiny ascending aorta
Coronary and brachiocephalic vessels fill backwards from arch
Ductal closure stops cerebral and coronary perfusion abruptly

steps.say: The first operation, done in the opening days of life, rebuilds a brand new aorta out of the pulmonary trunk.
steps.tx: Palliation starts with **Norwood Stage 1**. Norwood Stage 1, performed in the first week, creates an unobstructed neo aorta using the pulmonary trunk with atrial septectomy (removal of the atrial septum for unobstructed pulmonary venous return) and a systemic to pulmonary shunt, either a modified Blalock Taussig shunt or a Sano right ventricle to pulmonary artery conduit.

rows: Pulmonary trunk anastomosed to tiny ascending aorta
Unobstructed systemic outflow from single ventricle
Unimpeded pulmonary venous return to the heart
Modified BT shunt or Sano conduit
Controlled pulmonary blood flow for oxygenation

steps.say: One shunt variant takes blood straight from the ventricle through a small tube, which protects the coronaries from being robbed in diastole.
steps.tx: The conduit option is the **Sano modification (Sano vs BT shunt)**. The Sano modification uses a non valved PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene synthetic) conduit from the right ventricle to the pulmonary artery bifurcation, eliminating systemic diastolic steal and preserving coronary perfusion at the cost of a right ventriculotomy scar.

left.title: Modified BT Shunt
points: Gore-Tex tube from subclavian artery to pulmonary artery
Continuous run off lowers diastolic pressure and coronary filling
No ventricular incision with simpler shunt takedown later

right.title: Sano RV to PA Conduit
points: Non valved PTFE conduit from ventricle to pulmonary bifurcation
Diastolic pressure preserved so coronaries fill normally
Ventriculotomy scar may impair later ventricular function

steps.say: At a few months old the upper body veins are plumbed directly into the lungs, letting the single ventricle offload half its work.
steps.tx: Stage two is the **bidirectional Glenn (Glenn Stage 2)**. Bidirectional cavopulmonary shunt (the Glenn procedure) anastomoses the superior vena cava directly to the right pulmonary artery at **4-6 months** of age, so upper body venous return flows passively into both lungs without ventricular pumping.

nodes.label: Superior vena cava divided from the right atrium at 4 to 6 months
Caval end anastomosed to the superior aspect of right pulmonary artery
Upper body venous blood flows passively to both lungs
Single ventricle now handles only lower body and coronary return

steps.say: By preschool age the lower body veins join the same passive circuit, completing a circulation with no pump behind the lungs at all.
steps.tx: Completion is the **extracardiac Fontan (Fontan Stage 3)**. Extracardiac conduit total cavopulmonary connection (the Fontan) routes inferior vena cava blood to the pulmonary arteries at **2-4 years**, completing passive single ventricle venous return in which systemic venous pressure alone drives pulmonary blood flow.

rows: Secure systemic outflow with controlled pulmonary flow
Complete passive venous return to the lungs

steps.say: Surgeons deliberately leave a tiny escape hole in the Fontan circuit, trading a trace of blueness for a safer cardiac output.
steps.tx: Circuit safety uses a **Fontan fenestration of 4-5 mm**. A **4-5 mm** fenestration between the Fontan conduit and the atrium acts as a pop off valve to maintain systemic cardiac output at the cost of mild cyanosis, decompressing the high pressure venous circuit during exertion or pulmonary hypertensive crises.

left.title: Benefits of Fenestration
points: Maintains ventricular preload and cardiac output under stress
Shortens pleural drainage time after Fontan completion
Rescue pathway during pulmonary hypertensive episodes

right.title: Costs of Fenestration
points: Persistent right to left shunt with resting saturations of 85 to 90 percent
Paradoxical embolus risk requiring long term anticoagulation
May need device closure years later once pressures settle

steps.say: Years later the price of a pump less lung circuit appears in the gut and the airways, where high venous pressure weeps protein and casts.
steps.tx: Late failure brings **protein losing enteropathy**. Protein losing enteropathy and plastic bronchitis (rubbery airway casts) are severe late complications of chronically elevated central venous pressure in failing Fontan physiology, presenting with oedema, diarrhoea, hypoalbuminaemia, and recurrent cast expectoration needing transplant evaluation.
